chapter_theme: Akananuru 281 to 300, in the anthology's fixed order of lands: ten paalai poems weigh the wealth-road against the woman left behind, mostly from the man's side as he speaks to his own heart on the way (her rites of waiting, her farewell, her offer to come), with two elopements urged and blessed by the friend; hill poems press for marriage through the father's consent, the shut-in girl and the dreaded veri rite; neythal and marutham poems use Thondi, Korkai and Koodal as measures of pallor and gossip, and the friend turns maxims and hospitality into ways of binding the lover.

281.reading: The woman asks her friend what she should do: the man who spoke boldly of his manhood went off without fear that his word would prove false, a peacock's shed feather wound on his bow, across the rock the Moriyar's wheels cut on their march south with the Vadugar in the van, leaving her only gossip loud as a beaten drum.
281.nuance: The bow wound with peacock feather and the Moriyar's rock-cut pass are the very images Akananuru 69 uses to promise a quick return; here they describe a man already gone, and the only thing he has left behind is talk. The Moriyar road is history used as distance: he has gone as far as an emperor's army once came.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளது வேறுபாடு கண்டு ஆற்றாளாகிய தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: she speaks of a man who has crossed the rock-cut pass and left her

comparisons.tenor: the gossip he left behind, spread aloud through the town

occasion.words: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளது வேறுபாடு கண்டு ஆற்றாளாகிய தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது

282.reading: Within the hero's hearing, the friend tells the woman that their father has agreed to give her to the hill-lord whose hunters bring down ivory, gold, gems and pearls together; the gossiping town now speaks on his side, the mother praises his shoulders and says he is the one, and they themselves fold their fingers to the house god praying that the fixed day come quickly.
282.nuance: The three kinds of mountain wealth carried down together on a sandal-wood pole read like the bride-gifts the man should bring, and the poem is meant to be overheard: everyone has consented, so the only delay left is his. Even the alar that threatened secret love has turned to approval.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிக்கண் தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்ச் சொல்லியது. தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியதுமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: hunters, vengai garland and mountain slopes of the hill country

comparisons.tenor: pearls spilled from the broken elephant tusk

occasion.words: இரவுக்குறிக்கண் தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்ச் சொல்லியது

283.reading: The friend tells the man who has resolved to take the woman away with him that she is eager to go, and asks him not to think the road too hard; she wishes the rains to fall on the long forest so that its heat is quenched, grass springs up and the red velvet mites streak the cool ground like tufts of dyed cotton, making the way sweet for her to leave hardship and go with him.
283.nuance: The friend's blessing is a wish that the paalai road turn into mullai: rain, new grass and the red mites of the wet season. The village women who give scant food and the owl's thin cry belong to the hard road she hopes will soften.

colophon.thurai: உடன்போக்கு வலித்த தோழி தலைமகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: she will leave home to go with him

comparisons.tenor: the red mites scattered on the cool ground

284.reading: The man, his work done, says that the town of the fair woman whose love is more distracted than his own lies in the lovely forest where the small-eyed hare eats swollen varagu ears, sleeps curled, and wakes to go with its mate and drink at a little pool in a doorway, where millet-fed bowmen hunt deer in the jasmine gardens.
284.nuance: The whole first half is the home country seen with longing as he nears it; the hare that rises and goes off with its partner is the image of what he is about to do. The last lines turn the usual complaint around: he grants that her longing is greater than his.

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றிய தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது. தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியதுமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: jasmine gardens, scrub forest and varagu millet of the pasture land

iraicchi.act: the hare wakes from sleep and goes off with its mate to drink
iraicchi.sense: the man, his work done, will now go back to live beside his wife

285.reading: The friend, having won the woman's consent to elope, says that where they once grieved that the men would go and leave them, now the lover has said that she too will come with them through the desert where the red dog cuts down a stag to feed its hungry mate, travellers in stone-torn rags climb trees and the vulture watches; so come, friend, let us embrace many times.
285.nuance: The road is described at its cruellest just as the friend announces joy: the grief of being left is undone by the decision to go together. The red dog hunting for its mate shows the provision the man will make for her on that road.

colophon.thurai: 1உடன்போக்குடன் படுவித்த தோழி, தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the scorched desert road

comparisons.tenor: the travellers' rags torn by thrown stones

iraicchi.act: the male wild dog kills a stag to end the hunger of its mate
iraicchi.sense: the man who takes her through that land will provide for her as the beast does for its mate

286.reading: When the man takes her hand as if swearing, the friend, addressing him as lord of the cool-ford town where girls pound sand in the kaanchi shade and a kingfisher full of fish sleeps on a marutham branch, says the great hold back even what the heart desires, weigh virtue and wealth and their own worth, and only then carry out what they intended; if falsehood appears even in men like him, where is truth to be found in the world?
286.nuance: She raises him to the rank of the great precisely so that a broken promise would be a failure of truth for the whole world; the maxim is a trap built to hold him to his oath of marriage. Her reading of his gesture as an oath is the colophon's point.

colophon.thurai: வரைந் தெய்துவலென்று நீங்குந் தலைமகன் தலைமகளை ஆற்று வித்துக் கொண்டிருத்தல் வேண்டுமென்று தோழியைக் கைப் பற்றியது. தன்னைத் தொட்டுச் சூளுறுவானாகக் கருதித் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: marutham tree, kaanchi shade and cool ford of the river town

comparisons.tenor: the white sand heaped by the girls
what one has heard from the wise, restraining desire as a goad turns an elephant

occasion.words: தன்னைத் தொட்டுச் சூளுறுவானாகக் கருதித் தோழி சொல்லியது

287.reading: On the road, the man asks his heart whether the poor woman suffers at home, praying with bunched fingers and a vow-bound heart for company by day, while he toils on the endless way through deserted hamlets where the shrine has forgotten its daily offering, the west wind scatters a pair of doves from a banyan, a doe licks a stag's back and the herd gazes at thin shade as evening comes on.
287.nuance: The abandoned shrine that has forgotten its daily offering sits beside the woman who keeps her daily vow: the desert is full of things given up, while she is not. The pair of doves driven apart by the wind and the doe comforting the stag frame the two kinds of pairing he has in mind.

colophon.thurai: பிரிந்து போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் இடைச்சுரத்து நின்ற தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the endless dry way and the abandoned hamlets

iraicchi.act: the doe licks the back of her stag in the heat of the road
iraicchi.sense: even beasts on that road soothe their partners, while he has left her to bear her pain alone

288.reading: On a day meeting the friend tells the hill man, who comes daily in sandal paste and a vengai garland and has made light of them on finding them alone, that he may go; their father now guards the sweet-voiced girl as closely as the sacred mango grove of the hill goddesses on the cold slope, where even a monkey father who touches a fruit to feed his hungry mate is struck with sickness.
288.nuance: She tells him the girl is now shut in (செறிப்பு) without saying so: her guarded state is a forbidden grove where touching brings affliction. The monkey that cannot even take a fruit for its mate is the hero who can no longer reach her unless he marries.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறிக்கண் தோழி செறிப்பறிவு றீ இ வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: vengai of the slope, millet field and monkeys of the hill

comparisons.tenor: the father's guard over the girl, which none may touch without harm

289.reading: On a desert way of arrow-killed travellers' cairns and tall hero-stones given daily offerings, the man who has set his mind on his work asks his heart whether the girl who fretted if his embrace loosened even a little now sits dazed on her feathered bed, watching the wall where she marks the days, tears falling on her breast like pearls off a slack string, praying 'speak good' each time the lizard chirps, and fighting the dull evening.
289.nuance: Everything he imagines her doing (scoring the days on the wall, praying at the lizard's call) is the ritual of waiting, matched against the stones on his road that receive their own daily offering: both she and the dead are kept by daily rites.

colophon.thurai: பிரிந்து போகா நின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச்சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a desert way marked with cairns and hero-stones

comparisons.tenor: her tears falling on her breast

occasion.words: பிரிந்து போகா நின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச்சொல்லியது

290.reading: With the man listening outside at night, the woman asks her friend why, though he came alone with an unwavering heart to the backwater grove even before marrying her, her eyes, once lovely as the cool neythal of Kuttuvan's Thondi harbour, have lost their sapphire beauty and taken on the hue of gold, in his shore where a heron hen whose mate was caught in the fisher boys' net refuses food at evening and cries clutching her chick.
290.nuance: 'Even before marrying' turns the question into a warning: if he wastes her like this now, what after? The neythal of Thondi, the emblem of Kuttuvan's port, is what her eyes have stopped resembling.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக் குறிக்கண் தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore lord, backwater grove, neythal flower and heron

comparisons.tenor: the former dark beauty of her eyes
the pallor her eyes have taken

occasion.words: இரவுக் குறிக்கண் தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது

iraicchi.act: the heron hen whose mate is caught refuses food and cries at nightfall holding her chick
iraicchi.sense: in his own shore a bird fasts and cries for a lost mate, so he should see what his delay does to the woman

291.reading: The man going for wealth tells his heart, live long, that crossing the sun-scorched desert where the sky has withheld its rain, pebbles glitter like fireflies on slopes where an elephant fought a tiger, leaf-crowned robbers with arrows humming like bees seize the caravans' goods, and a stag with new horns in velvet calls out meaning to feed its spotted doe, it has remembered the fine beauty of their beloved's hair, eyes and shoulders.
291.nuance: The heart's remembering is blessed (வாழிய) rather than rebuked: the desert has not driven her out of his mind. The stag that has lost its old horns and calls for its doe is the one tender thing on the road.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் இடைச்சுரத்துத் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: ponds dried and the hard desert

comparisons.tenor: the pebbles glittering everywhere on the slope

iraicchi.act: the stag with broken horns calls out, thinking to feed his spotted doe
iraicchi.sense: the man too, far on the road, thinks of the one he means to provide for

292.reading: The woman, afraid of the veri rite, asks her friend what to do: mother has misread her loosened bangles and spends wealth in worry, and if the stranger velan, to kill a kid not yet weaned, sways in his garland she will be ashamed, all because the lord of the hill, where a hunter's sling-stone flung at a night-grazing elephant flies off scattering vengai blooms and honey and lodges in a jackfruit, has not married her.
292.nuance: The sling-stone that misses the elephant and ends in the jackfruit, wrecking flowers and honey on its way, may be read as the mother's rite aimed at the wrong cause; but the poem gives no second correspondence firm enough to make it a hidden comparison, so it is left as scene.

colophon.thurai: வெறியச்சுறீஇத் தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: hunter, vengai and the hill country

293.reading: The woman tells her friend that they say he will go alone through the summer desert, where a dead leafless tree is netted with spider webs, heat shimmers like spread silk and dark fruits like gem-coins fall, and they say that she, aching like a calf tied apart from its mother by heartless herdsmen, will only speak bitter words; what has confused their lover?
293.nuance: Twice 'they say' (என்ப): the plan to leave reaches her as report, and so does the prediction of how she will take it. The calf penned away from its mother is a mullai image brought into the desert to name her helplessness.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் பிரியக்கருதிய தலைமகன் குறிப்பறிந்து தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது. தலைமகனாற் பிரிவுணர்த்தப்பட்ட தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: summer heat of the desert

comparisons.tenor: the dead tree netted with spider webs

comparisons.vehicle: பண்பில் கோவலர் தாய்பிரித்து யாத்த நெஞ்சமர் குழவி

294.reading: To the friend who urges patience as the season comes, the woman says that after the thunder and downpour, with karuvilai flowers wet like the eyes of women left by their lovers, eengai shoots glistening as if dipped in ghee, avarai thick in flower and ripe paddy bowing in the fields, at midnight in the dewy season, lashed by the north wind and wondering whether the men who know nothing of her pain, kept in the angry king's war camp, will ever come, she cannot bear her loneliness.
294.nuance: The season she was promised has come and every plant shows it, including the flowers that look like weeping women; the comfort the friend offers is undone by the very signs that were meant to bring him. The king's camp names a war, not wealth, as the cause of his absence.

colophon.thurai: பருவவரவின்கண் வற்புறுக்குந் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits in the rains for a man kept in the king's camp

comparisons.vehicle: காதலர்ப் பிரிந்த கையறு மகளிர் நீர்வார் கண்ணின்

295.reading: The friend tells the woman whose shoulders have taken on affliction that though he has crossed the waterless forest where a tusker that beat a tiger stands weary beside its cow, the salt-merchants' well dug for passing travellers, the hill of Pulli and the land beyond where the Vadugar archers shout over toddy and the language changes, he will bring back her flawless beauty.
295.nuance: Pulli's hill is the edge of the known world in these poems; beyond it the speech itself changes. The friend's comfort measures his distance precisely in order to say it does not matter.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: springs dried in the lingering summer

iraicchi.act: the weary tusker, its musth spent, stays beside its cow in the dry forest
iraicchi.sense: even in drought the beast keeps by its mate, so the man who went through that land is bound to her and will return

296.reading: The friend refusing the man entry says he slept yesterday in the fragrant grove with the dark girl who wears kaanchi pollen in her hair, bathed with her today in the great Vaigai, and comes with his chest still wet: can he hide it from them, when it has fallen into many mouths and become gossip like the swelling clamour of Koodal, the hill-high city of Chezhiyan, lord of Korkai where pearl oysters are traded for toddy?
296.nuance: The proof against him is bodily (the undried chest), and the gossip is measured against the ordinary noise of the Pandya capital, not a battle: his affair is as public as Madurai's markets.

colophon.thurai: வாயில்வேண்டிச் சென்ற தலைமகற்கு வாயின்மறுக்குந் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend reproaches a husband who has been with another woman

occasion.words: வாயில்வேண்டிச் சென்ற தலைமகற்கு வாயின்மறுக்குந் தோழி சொல்லியது

297.reading: Going for wealth, the man asks his heart what will become of her grief, which overflows at midnight and the dull evening, and of the shy glad look of the girl who said she would come with him through the fearful forest where travellers pass by an old hero-stone without stopping to read its worn inscription, a wildcat's kitten follows its mother like stars round the moon, and the warriors' raiding drum makes the vulture shift its wings.
297.nuance: The hero-stone's letters, carved to keep a name, are now passed unread by weary travellers: the road is a place where even fame is forgotten, and he fears forgetting is not what she will do. Her offer to come with him is the elopement he refused.

colophon.thurai: பொருள்வயிற் போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the fearful forest with its old hero-stones

comparisons.tenor: the kitten keeping close to its mother

occasion.words: பொருள்வயிற் போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

iraicchi.act: the wildcat's kitten keeps close at its mother's side as stars ring the moon
iraicchi.sense: she wanted to keep as close to him on this road, which is why her offer to come haunts him

298.reading: At a midnight meeting the woman tells the lord of the hill, where vengai shoots glow like the sun rising from the full sea, that his coming here through the tusker-haunted forest path, white spear in hand and bees on his garland, is sweet, yet out of fear that her mother would learn of it she has kept her love unspoken, and the sleepless friend who shares her nights has gladly assured her he will not delay.
298.nuance: The lines are tangled: she seems to weigh his dangerous night visit against the friend's comfort that he will soon come for good. What she will not say aloud is the point: her love is guarded by fear of the house.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிக்கண் தலைமகற்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: vengai, tusker and the hill lord

comparisons.tenor: the bright shoots of the flowering vengai

299.reading: On the road the man tells his heart that though they might live forgetting home, they cannot forget how she took the news of his going through the forest where wind-blown teak leaves fly like screaming kites: her face bowed like the waning moon, tears falling on her breast, unable to stand, she hid in her hair and, sighing, wished his going well in faltering words.
299.nuance: Her blessing on his journey is the most painful thing he remembers: she says what a wife should say, with every sign of her body saying the opposite.

colophon.thurai: இடைச்சுரத்துப் போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the wide desert way

comparisons.tenor: the teak leaves whirled up by the wind

occasion.words: இடைச்சுரத்துப் போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது

300.reading: The friend tells the man leaving a day meeting on the shore that the girl wept bitterly when he bade her go home, and she fears that if he parts like a stranger the girl will come to harm; so let him arrive at their busy hamlet as if from afar, and their kin will receive him, say the ford is dark and the tide brings sharks and press him to stay, and they will make him a welcome guest of the house, if he will only consent.
300.nuance: The friend writes a little play: the lover arrives as a stranger and is kept for the night as a guest, a way of bringing him under the family's roof before marriage. Hospitality is turned into a step toward varaivu.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி வந்து நீங்குந் தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen, the shore grove and sharks of the sea coast

occasion.words: பகற்குறி வந்து நீங்குந் தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது

links.note: Both set the man's road at the rock the Moriyar's wheels cut and arm him with a bow wound with a peacock's shed feather; in 69 the friend says he will not delay, in 281 the woman says he went without fear of breaking his word.
links.teaches: The same stock road and the same feathered bow serve one poet as a promise of return and another as proof of desertion, so the image fixed the distance while the speaker decided what the distance meant.

links.note: Purananuru 175 likens a patron's lasting charity to the rock-cut pass of the Moriyar's chariot wheels, a public way open to all; Akananuru 281 sends the lover over that same pass.
links.teaches: In praise poetry the Moriyar's cut road stands for something permanent and shared, while the akam poet uses it as the point past which a man is lost to one woman, so one piece of remembered history carried opposite values in the two kinds of poetry.

links.note: Both use the beaten drum (அறைபறை) for love exposed to the town while the man is away; in the Kural it is her own eyes, in 281 it is the gossip he left behind.
links.teaches: The Kural takes the stock drum of gossip and turns it on the woman's own eyes, so the pairing shows the couplet moving the blame for exposure from the town, as the Sangam poem has it, to her own body.

links.note: Kural 467 says to deliberate and then resolve, never resolve and then deliberate; the friend in 286 says the great weigh virtue, wealth and their own worth before carrying out what they intend.
links.teaches: The poem shows the Kural's rule of deliberate action used as a lever in courtship: if the great think before they promise, a lover who swore cannot later plead haste, so the maxim becomes a way to bind a promise.

links.note: In 61 the friend tells the woman not to grieve gazing at the wall scored with the days; in 289 the man on the road imagines her looking at that wall.
links.teaches: The wall marked with the days of absence was known to both sides of the parting: the man can picture the very ritual the friend tries to stop, so his guilt in 289 rests on a convention the woman's side also names.

links.note: Purananuru 48 says Thondi smells of the neythal flowers blooming in its great backwater; Akananuru 290 says the woman's eyes were once like the great cool neythal of Kuttuvan's Thondi harbour.
links.teaches: Thondi's neythal was the town's own emblem in praise of its king, so when the akam poet says her eyes have lost that likeness he is measuring her pallor against a flower the audience knew as Thondi's pride.

links.note: Both are Mamoolanar's: in 61 the man would not stay even for Pulli's festive Venkadam; in 295 he has gone past Pulli's hill into the Vadugar country where the language changes.
links.teaches: Read together, the poet's Pulli's hill is the last familiar landmark: one poem stops at it as the measure of a great prize, the other goes beyond it to a land of strange speech, giving his geography of absence an inner and an outer edge.

links.note: Both are marutham poems in which the friend refuses the husband and compares the gossip about him to noise at Chezhiyan's Koodal; in 116 it is louder than the shout of the battlefield where he routed two kings, in 296 it is like the city's everyday clamour.
links.teaches: The akam poets measured scandal by the noise of the Pandya capital in war and in peace alike, so Koodal's fame worked as a ready scale for how far gossip had spread.

links.note: Purananuru 264 tells of a hero-stone newly set up with his name engraved and crowned with a peacock feather; Akananuru 297 shows such a stone grown old, its inscribed name passed unread by weary travellers.
links.teaches: The puram poem records the moment a name is carved to outlast death, and the akam poem shows the same kind of stone generations on with no one reading it, so the pair qualifies the promise of the engraved name.

source_issues: 285: the colophon thurai begins with a stray footnote numeral, '1உடன்போக்குடன்'; copied as it stands.
288: the base text numbers the last line 27 and line 10 as 20 though the poem has 17 lines (misprinted numbers); line 16 reads கொங்தொடு, apparently a misprint for கொங்கொடு (with pollen).
291: line 1 reads வானம் யெல்வளம், which is not a Tamil word form (no word begins with யெ); probably a misprint, perhaps for பெயல்வளம் (the wealth of rain). Marked as the sky withholding its rain.
294: the base text has 16 lines, the commentary edition (pmuni0523_02) 17; marked as the base text stands.
295: the base text has 22 lines, the commentary edition (pmuni0523_02) 20; marked as the base text stands.
296: the poet is given as மதுரைப் ரோலவாயார், which cannot be right (no Tamil word begins with ர); a misprint for some other name, left as it is in the core record.
